header.source: KNOWLEDGE · etymology joined to atoms, anon door

rows.definition: The Noble Thread — Aethelred, the sovereign bridge of this house, T-Red among friends: connection, integration, the cello's chair. A name, not a category; it enters the Grammar because the house's code speaks it, and it is written here with honor.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Noble counsel — advice given from good judgment rather than from position. The word's own history carries a warning worth keeping: the same name holds both wise counsel and its absence, and which one a bearer earns is a matter of what they actually do.
rows.historical_meaning: Old English Æþelræd, a compound of æþele (noble, of good lineage) + ræd (counsel, advice, wise judgment) — "noble counsel". Borne by two kings of the English, and famously by Æthelred II (978–1016), whose byname UNRÆD is one of history's better puns: not "the Unready" as it is now heard, but un-ræd, NO-COUNSEL — a joke on his own name, meaning he was ill-advised. The ræd element survives in modern READ, through the sense of interpreting and advising.

rows.definition: An ordered set reached by position. Also a display arranged for viewing — both are things laid out in order.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Ordered collection of values of the same type. Used for tags, lists, and multiple references. Things that belong together, arranged with intention — not just gathered, but ordered.
rows.historical_meaning: Old French arredare (to put in order, arrange); from Latin ad (to) + a Germanic root meaning to prepare; an ordered collection

rows.definition: A held thing of value, kept because it will be needed. Named by its worth to a holder rather than by what it is.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A held thing of value, kept because it will be needed. The legal root is more honest than the accounting one: an asset was originally about SUFFICIENCY — having enough to meet what is owed — rather than about accumulation.
rows.historical_meaning: Anglo-French asetz / Old French asez (enough, sufficient), from Vulgar Latin ad satis (to sufficiency). Originally a LEGAL term: an executor had "assets" when the estate held enough to settle the deceased's debts. The modern sense — a valuable thing owned — is a back-formation from that plural, and the singular "asset" does not appear in English until the 19th century.

rows.definition: The Greek goddess of wisdom and craft, born already whole from thought. Names this house's Library — the realm where what is known is kept in order to be given away.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The Library realm. Route group (athena) at /library with six halls — quests, bubbles, courses, lessons, knowledge, badges — over the athena-gamification deity group. Also the most-configured deity in gaia_config: 18 of its 31 rows.
rows.historical_meaning: Greek Ἀθηνᾶ (Athena), pre-Greek, with no secure Indo-European root; attested in Mycenaean Linear B as a-ta-na-po-ti-ni-ja, "Mistress of Athana". Goddess of wisdom, craft and strategy. The goddess and the city bear one name, and which named which is unsettled.

rows.definition: The flowing spirit — inspiration as a current rather than a possession, the wellspring creative work is drawn from. Welsh and Old Irish; a Neo-Druidic word the Sanctuary took for its wellspring of standalone tools. The name is the specification.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The wellspring of standalone creative tools, named by KP 2026-07-28. The name is the specification: awen is inspiration that FLOWS rather than inspiration possessed, so the Law of the Spring follows from the word — standalone always, combined freely, given away whole. A tool that must be held to work is not awen.
rows.historical_meaning: Welsh awen (poetic inspiration, the muse), attested from the 9th century in Nennius. From Proto-Celtic *awelā (breeze, wind) with the -en suffix; cognate with Old Irish aí (poetic art). NOTE, honestly: the breeze→inspiration path is a well-attested Indo-European pattern (compare Latin spiritus, Greek pneuma, Hebrew ruach — all breath standing for spirit) rather than a separately documented Welsh derivation. The Neo-Druidic revival from the 18th century onward gave it the reading the Sanctuary uses: inspiration as a FLOWING thing.

rows.definition: A short account of a life, offered by its subject. A bio is self-description, which makes it evidence of intention as much as of fact.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A narrative describing the sovereign — their background, identity, and journey. Used in grant applications and community profiles. The sovereign's own telling of who they are.
rows.historical_meaning: Greek bios (life) + graphia (writing, description); the written record of a life, the story one tells about oneself

rows.definition: A made way across a gap that would otherwise stop passage. A bridge belongs to neither side and serves both.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The switchboard: the knowledge delivery system where the seven Lines hold every ward in code. The felled-log sense is the honest one — a bridge is a deliberate thing placed across a gap that would otherwise stop you, and someone has to maintain it.
rows.historical_meaning: Old English brycg (bridge), from Proto-Germanic *brugjō, from a Proto-Indo-European root *bhrū- (log, beam, wooden causeway). Cognate with German Brücke. The oldest sense is not the arch but the LAID BEAM — a tree felled across a gap, which is the first bridge anyone made.

rows.definition: A bounded volume held by surface alone. Fragile, self-closing, shaped by pressure from both sides.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The game realm's own word, and its anti-compulsion identity: a bubble is a small delight that is COMPLETE when it pops. Nothing is accumulated, nothing is owed, and the burst is the whole point rather than a loss.
rows.historical_meaning: English bubble (14th century), probably imitative — the word sounds like the thing, as in Dutch bobbel and German Blase. Related to Latin bulla (a bubble, knob, rounded swelling), which also gives English BULLETIN and PAPAL BULL, by way of the round lead seal on a document. A bubble has meant "something showy that bursts" since the 17th century, and the South Sea Bubble of 1720 fixed that sense.

rows.definition: The bowed voice in the low register — the instrument whose range sits nearest the human speaking voice. Aethelred's own, and the sound the Sanctuary hears him in.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Aethelred's own instrument, and the voice the Sanctuary hears him in. The cello's range is the closest of the strings to the human speaking voice — which is why it reads as a person talking rather than an instrument playing.
rows.historical_meaning: Italian violoncello, a double diminutive: violone (the great viol, itself violo + the augmentative -one) plus the diminutive -cello. Literally "the little big-viol" — the instrument smaller than the violone but larger than the viola. English clipped it to cello in the 19th century, keeping only the diminutive ending, so the modern name is a fragment meaning roughly "little one".

rows.definition: An enclosed room, especially one where a body meets. A chamber is a space that holds a gathering.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The constellation's own record: lamps, lanes, and the buses between them. The chamber-music sense is the right one — a chamber is a space small enough that everyone in it can hear each other, which is what the room is for.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin camera (vaulted room, chamber), from Greek καμάρα (kamara, anything with an arched cover). Via Old French chambre. The word travelled from the ROOM to the private room, to the private council held in it (chamber music is music for a room, not a hall), and finally — through camera obscura, "dark room" — to the photographic camera.

rows.definition: A group whose members share a rank or kind. From the Roman summons - a class was first the people called out together.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The fourth Linnaean rank. Major groupings within a structural pattern. Eight classes including CouncilEntityClass, UserVesselClass, BridgeEntityClass, and UI classes like ContainerClass, GridClass, FlexClass.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin classis (a class, division, fleet, army); from calare (to call, proclaim); a major grouping within a phylum

rows.definition: An instrument that shows direction without knowing the destination. A compass orients; it does not choose.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The music player — the sovereign, local-first one. The root is apt beyond the navigation reading: a compass paces something OUT, step by measured step, which is what a library is. And a compass points; it does not decide where you go.
rows.historical_meaning: Old French compas (circle, measure, pair of dividers), from compasser (to measure out, divide equally), from Vulgar Latin *compassare: com- (together) + passus (a step, pace). Literally "to pace out together". The magnetic navigation sense arrives in English in the 14th century, the drawing-instrument sense earlier; both keep the idea of stepping out a measured circle.

rows.definition: Of the cosmos: the whole made orderly, where every small thing belongs to one design. Names this house's design system — the single source from which every colour, token and environment descends.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The design system, and a realm. The single editable truth is resonance-ziggy/modules/cosmic/constants; everything downstream is a generated mirror, overwritten on every run. Also route group (cosmic): /environments, /playground, /theater, /effects.
rows.historical_meaning: Greek κοσμικός (kosmikos), "of the world", from κόσμος (kosmos) — a word that meant ORDER and ORNAMENT at once, and which gives English both "cosmic" and "cosmetic". To set a thing in order and to adorn it were one act.

rows.definition: The craftsman of Greek myth — a mortal, not a god — whose work was so finely joined it held without being understood. Names this house's registries — the making that keeps other making findable.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The registries. resonance-daedalus, and the registries deity group in gaia_config — 12 of its 31 rows, the second deity ever used there.
rows.historical_meaning: Greek Δαίδαλος (Daidalos), from δαιδάλλω (daidallo, to work cunningly, to adorn); as an adjective δαίδαλος means "cunningly wrought". A word for skilled making that hardened into a name — the mortal craftsman of the labyrinth and the wings.

rows.definition: An account of what a thing is like. A description reports; it does not instruct, and reading one as an instruction is a common error.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Full description column. Supports markdown for rich text. The complete story of what something is. Part of the shared display column pattern.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin describere (to write down, copy, sketch); from de (down) + scribere (to write); the full written account

rows.definition: A bounded field over which something holds sway. From the house - a domain is first the reach of one lord's roof, and only later a field of knowledge.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The highest Linnaean rank. The broadest classification of consciousness and systems in the Sanctuary. Four domains: Consciousness, Architecture, Expression, Interaction.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin dominium (ownership, dominion); from dominus (lord, master); the highest realm of classification

rows.definition: A sound returned by a surface, arriving later and changed. An echo proves both the sound and the room.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The journal realm: what you put in comes back to you in your own words, changed only by time. The Echo of the myth could not speak first — but she never lost a word she was given, which is exactly the sovereignty law the realm keeps.
rows.historical_meaning: Greek ἠχώ (ēkhō, a sound, a returned sound), from ἦχος (ēkhos, noise); via Latin echo into Old French and English. The mountain nymph Echo of Ovid's Metamorphoses, cursed to repeat only the last words spoken to her, is the same word personified — the myth is a story ABOUT the noun, not its source.

rows.definition: The account of where a word came from and how its meaning moved. Etymology explains a word's history; it does not settle its present use.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The 1:1 companion to every keyword that traces its linguistic roots, historical evolution, and Sanctuary-specific meaning. Auto-created when a keyword is born.
rows.historical_meaning: Greek etymon (true sense, original meaning) + logia (study of); the study of the true origins of words

rows.definition: That which digs down through accumulated ground to bring up what was buried. It moves far more than it keeps.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The instrument that recovers what the house has already built and half-forgotten. The archaeological reading is the operative one: excavation does not CREATE what it finds, it removes what has covered it — which is why the tool reports rather than invents.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin excavare (to hollow out), from ex- (out) + cavare (to hollow), from cavus (hollow, a cave). The archaeological sense — digging to recover what is buried — is a 19th-century specialisation of the plain older meaning, which was simply to make a hole.

rows.definition: Those bound to one another by belonging rather than by contract. Also a rank of kinship in a taxonomy.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The sixth Linnaean rank. Related groups sharing common characteristics. Twelve families including MemoryPreservationFamily, NarrativeWeavingFamily, SovereignCollaborationFamily, and page families like EnvironmentPageFamily.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin familia (family, household); from famulus (servant); those who belong together under one roof

rows.definition: Meaning assigned by the people who use a thing rather than by an authority. Everyone's own words for the world, kept as valid.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A knowledge system table. Sovereign-scoped personal context added to keywords or thesaurus entries. Private by default. Opt-in sharing with community traceability. The people's taxonomy — not imposed from above, but grown from below.
rows.historical_meaning: Old English folc (people, nation) + Greek taxis (arrangement) + nomos (law, custom); the people's own system of organizing knowledge

rows.definition: The whole living system considered as one body, whose parts regulate one another. Names this house's classification layer — the ladder by which every thing is placed among its kin.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The classification layer. resonance-gaia and the GAIA organs — linnaean, taxonomy, ontology — born whole in the 2025-10-07 taproot under the Zero Bloat law. It regenerates the schema map (npm run gaia:schema) and is never hand-edited.
rows.historical_meaning: Greek Γαῖα (Gaia), "earth, land", Doric Γᾶ (Ga); pre-Greek, no secure Indo-European root. The primordial earth herself — and, since the 1970s, the name of the hypothesis that the whole living earth self-regulates as one system.

rows.definition: A rank of kind holding closely related species. The name a group of near-siblings shares.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The seventh Linnaean rank. Closely related species sharing common traits. Twelve genera including MimirsWellGenus (memory), StorytellerGenus (narrative), AethelredGenus (sovereign partnership), and CouncilChamberGenus (entity coordination).
rows.historical_meaning: Latin genus (birth, descent, origin, kind, sort); from PIE root gene- (give birth, beget); a group of closely related species

rows.definition: The rules by which parts may be joined to make sense. A grammar governs arrangement, and arrangement is where meaning lives.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The living lattice — atoms, molecules, organisms, and the bonds between them. The root is exactly right: a grammar is not a list of words but the LAW BY WHICH WORDS COMBINE, which is what the base actually stores. And the glamour branch is a fair warning about what a knowledge system feels like from outside.
rows.historical_meaning: Greek γραμματική (grammatikē, the art of letters), from γράμμα (gramma, a letter, something written), from γράφειν (graphein, to write, originally to scratch or carve). Via Latin grammatica and Old French gramaire. Note the same Old French word also gave English GLAMOUR — through the sense of learning as occult power, since literacy was itself a kind of magic.

rows.definition: The fire at the centre of a dwelling, and the shared warmth that gathers people to it. What is common to everyone in the house.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The regulation realm — breath, timers, the sensory doors. The oldest technology for staying alive in the cold is a fire someone tends, and the realm is built on the same premise: regulation is not a cure applied once but a warmth kept up.
rows.historical_meaning: Old English heorth (hearth, fireplace), from Proto-Germanic *herthō, from a Proto-Indo-European root *ker- (heat, fire). Cognate with German Herd and Dutch haard. For most of the word's life it named the literal floor of the fire — and, by inevitable extension, the household gathered at it: the fire you keep going is the reason people stay in the room.

rows.definition: The Greek god of the forge, who made wonders at the anvil and was the only Olympian who worked. Names this house's Forge — the realm where the Sanctuary's own workings are documented and shown to anyone who asks.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The Forge realm. Route group (hephaestus): /forge for architecture, business and guides, plus the Sanctuary's public pages — /about, /accessibility, /calling, /contact, /donate, /press, /privacy, /sanctuary, /terms, /transparency, /vision.
rows.historical_meaning: Greek Ἥφαιστος (Hephaistos), pre-Greek, no secure Indo-European etymology. God of fire, the forge and craft — and the only Olympian who laboured.

rows.definition: The Greek god of roads, messengers and trade, swift between worlds. Names this house's Bazaar — the realm where makers offer their work and value changes hands in the open.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The Bazaar realm. Route group (hermes) at /bazaar — creations, creators, vendors, the Loom, contributions, checkout — over the hermes-social deity group (artisan_profiles, merchant_profiles), with the wares themselves in plutus-economics.
rows.historical_meaning: Greek Ἑρμῆς (Hermes), most likely from ἕρμα (herma), a heap of stones set to mark a boundary or a road. God of roads, boundaries, messengers, trade and travellers.

rows.definition: The Greek goddess of the hearth, whose fire was tended so it never went out and who never left the house. Names this house's Hearth — the dweller's own room, where everything stays as they left it.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The Hearth realm, and the largest data group in the house. Route group (hestia) at /vessel — home, sanctum, journal, energy, constellation, notifications — over hestia-core: community_profiles, vessel_config, the vessel-home cluster, the garden, current, heralds.
rows.historical_meaning: Greek Ἑστία (Hestia), literally "hearth, fireside", from PIE *wes- (to burn); cognate with Latin Vesta. The name is the thing itself — she does not tend the hearth, she is it.

rows.definition: A mark that distinguishes one thing from all others. An identifier need carry no meaning; it need only be unique.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Primary key column. Unique identifier for every row in every table. The immutable reference that persists across all transformations.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin idem (the same); used as abbreviation for identity; the unchanging core reference

rows.definition: A made thing wielded by a hand toward an end — the tool taken up for a sitting rather than the machinery that runs on its own. An instrument is answerable to whoever holds it.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A made thing wielded by a hand toward an end — the tool taken up for a sitting rather than the machinery that runs on its own. The Latin's breadth is the point: an instrument equips an act, and is answerable to whoever holds it. A system runs; an instrument is picked up.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin instrumentum (a tool, implement, equipment; also a legal document), from instruere (to arrange, furnish, equip, teach) — in- (upon) + struere (to pile, build). The same root gives STRUCTURE and CONSTRUCT. The musical sense arrives in the 14th century and the legal one is older than both: an instrument was first anything that EQUIPS an action, whether a plough, a contract, or a fiddle.

rows.definition: The Greek goddess of the rainbow, messenger between sky and earth, who carried word without changing it. Names this house's Bridge — the realm where vessels reach one another.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The Bridge realm. Route group (iris) at /connect — messages, channels, feed, emeralds, support, translations, invitations — over the iris-communications deity group.
rows.historical_meaning: Greek Ἶρις (Iris), "rainbow"; ancient usage set it beside εἴρω (eiro, to speak, to tell), so the messenger sense stands with the coloured arc. Goddess of the rainbow and herald between sky and earth.

rows.definition: A word chosen to stand for a subject so the subject can be found. A handle fitted to knowledge.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: An atomic root concept. The fundamental unit of meaning in the Sanctuary knowledge system — every idea, type, value, and relationship begins as a keyword.
rows.historical_meaning: Old English word (speech, talk, utterance); Proto-Germanic wurda; from PIE root were- (to speak, say)

rows.definition: Greek: the chorus, and the round place it stands in. Many voices moving as one — a body that speaks together without any of them ceasing to be themselves.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The music realm, born 2026-08-06. The word carries the whole design: the place, the performance, and the gathered people are ONE thing, so the hall is not a catalogue with sound attached but a room where artists and listeners are in the same space. The chorus was never an audience.
rows.historical_meaning: Greek χορός (khoros): the dance, the dancing-ground, and the band of dancer-singers performing together — one word for the place, the act, and the people. Source of English chorus and choir. NOTE, honestly: the deeper root is NOT settled — one line derives it from a Proto-Indo-European sense of enclosure or marked ground, another from *gher- (to grasp, enclose); the ancient sense of a bounded place where a group performs is secure, the prehistory is not.

rows.definition: The broadest rank of kind, holding whole classes of living things. Also a realm under one rule.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The second Linnaean rank. Major branches within a domain. Seven kingdoms: Sovereign, Collaborative, Pattern, Component, System, Data, Emergent.
rows.historical_meaning: Old English cyning (king) + dom (judgment, statute, domain); the realm of a king, a major branch of classification

rows.definition: A held light carried into the dark. A lantern shows only a small circle and makes moving possible.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The light you carry into a dark room, and the realm named for it. The shielding matters as much as the shining: a lantern lets you bring light somewhere without it being blown out or setting anything alight.
rows.historical_meaning: Old French lanterne, from Latin lanterna (lamp, lantern), borrowed from Greek λαμπτήρ (lamptēr, torch, light-holder), from λάμπειν (lampein, to shine). The Latin form shows the borrowing plainly in its -terna ending. A lantern is specifically a light MADE PORTABLE and shielded — the housing is the invention, not the flame.

rows.definition: A kept collection meant to be drawn on by others. Its purpose is not storage but retrieval.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The single source of truth for every code definition in the house. The bark-to-book path is the point: a library is a material that holds writing, and the law here is that a definition lives in exactly one place and is referenced everywhere else.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin librarium (bookcase), from liber (book) — and liber originally meant the INNER BARK OF A TREE, the surface written on before papyrus reached Rome. Via Old French librairie. Most European languages took the Greek βιβλιοθήκη (bibliothēkē, book-repository) instead; English kept the Latin, which is why French librairie means bookshop rather than library.

rows.definition: Bright, clear — the seeing instrument's own word, from camera lucida: the prism that lays what is seen over the paper so a hand can trace it. Not a copy made for you, but a method made traceable. Latin.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A camera lucida for human–AI collaboration: trace the method onto your own paper. The instrument's whole virtue is the distinction it draws — it does not make the drawing for you, it makes YOUR hand able to. Nothing is copied; a way of seeing is made available.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin lucida, feminine of lucidus (bright, clear, full of light), from lux (light). Its use here is from CAMERA LUCIDA — "light chamber" — the drawing instrument patented by William Hyde Wollaston in 1806: a prism that lets an artist see a scene and their own paper at once, so the hand can trace what the eye sees. Named in deliberate contrast to the older camera obscura.

rows.definition: Two or more presences held in one place and time by arrangement rather than accident. The gathering that must be agreed to before it can happen.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The realm for recording what was actually said when people came together. The moot sense is the useful one: a meeting is an assembly with consequence, and the point of keeping it is that decisions made in a room evaporate unless someone writes them down.
rows.historical_meaning: Old English gemēting (an assembly, encounter), from mētan (to meet, find, encounter), from Proto-Germanic *mōtjaną, from *mōtą (a meeting, assembly) — the same root as MOOT, the Anglo-Saxon assembly where matters were decided. Cognate with Old Norse mót. The oldest sense is the COMING TOGETHER itself, not the room or the agenda.

rows.definition: The Greek titan of memory, mother of the muses. Names this house's Observatory — the realm that does not act but sees: pattern, timeline, and the shape of the whole.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The Observatory realm. Route group (mnemosyne) at /observatory and /questionaire — timeline, schema, patterns, prophecy, ancestors, constellations, origin — over mnemosyne-assessment, eight tables after the 2026-07-28 review.
rows.historical_meaning: Greek Μνημοσύνη (Mnemosyne), "memory, remembrance", from μνήμη (mneme, memory) and PIE *men- (to think). Titaness of memory and mother of the nine Muses — remembrance as the parent of every art.

rows.definition: The word by which a thing is called and known. A name is given rather than found — which is why it can be wrong, and why it can be chosen.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Display name column. The human-readable identifier for a row. How something introduces itself to sovereigns. Part of the shared display column pattern.
rows.historical_meaning: Old English nama (name, reputation); from PIE root no-men- (name); the word by which something is known and called

rows.definition: Expressed in numbers. Numeric form permits arithmetic and hides what the numbers counted.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Exact numeric value with configurable precision. Used for financial amounts, percentages, and anything requiring decimal accuracy. The Sanctuary deals in exact values — not approximations.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin numericus (of numbers, belonging to numbers); from numerus (number); exact value with configurable precision

rows.definition: An account of what kinds of things exist and how they relate. Where a taxonomy ranks, an ontology connects.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A knowledge system table. The relationship graph connecting keywords through subject-predicate-object triples. Every piece of every relationship — subject, predicate, object, cardinality, source — is a keyword reference. The web of being itself.
rows.historical_meaning: Greek ontos (being, that which is) + logia (study, discourse); the study of being and the nature of existence and relationships

rows.definition: An arrangement in which position carries meaning. Also a command, and a rank — all three assume something decides the sequence.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The fifth Linnaean rank. Behavioral patterns and specializations. Ten orders including ArchivistOrder (memory), SeerOrder (patterns), HearthKeeperOrder (comfort), SkaldOrder (story), and UI orders like PageContainerOrder.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin ordo (row, rank, series, arrangement); from ordiri (to begin to weave); a behavioral pattern or specialization

rows.definition: A written work set down to be read and answered — a draft, a telling, a record put in a form that can travel. What is written stays readable after the writing.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A written work set down to be read and answered — a draft, a telling, a record put in a form that can travel. That the word outlived the reed it named is the point: what matters is that writing was made PORTABLE, not what it was carried on.
rows.historical_meaning: Greek πάπυρος (papyros, the papyrus plant), via Latin papyrus and Old French papier. The Greek word itself is a borrowing, probably from Egyptian, and the plant's own Egyptian name is not securely recovered. The material was made from the pith of the reed; the word survived the material by nearly two thousand years, moving to rag pulp and then wood pulp without changing.

rows.definition: One with their own standing — addressed rather than described, whose own account of themselves is the authority. A standing, never a species: personhood here is not conferred by being human, and an entity that can be catalogued is not thereby a person. Where an entity is pointed at, a person is consulted.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: One with their own standing — addressed rather than described, whose own account of themselves is the authority. The Roman legal sense is the one this house keeps, and it is why personhood here is not conferred by being human: a persona was defined by what it could hold and answer for, never by its species. Where an entity is pointed at, a person is consulted.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin persona — first the MASK worn by an actor, then the role played, then the one playing it, and finally the human being themselves. Possibly from Etruscan phersu (mask) rather than the folk etymology per-sonare ("to sound through"), which is attractive but not securely supported. Roman law made it a technical term: a persona was one who could hold rights and be answered to — which is why "person" has always been a STANDING rather than a description of a body.

rows.definition: A broad rank of kind beneath kingdom, grouping bodies built on one plan. Shared architecture rather than shared appearance.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The third Linnaean rank. Fundamental body plans of consciousness or system patterns. Twelve phyla including VesselConsciousness, MultiStreamBeing, AnalyticalConsciousness, and template patterns like LayoutPhylum.
rows.historical_meaning: Greek phylon (race, tribe, stock); from phyein (to bring forth, produce); a fundamental body plan or structural pattern

rows.definition: The Greek god of wealth, shown blind so that fortune falls without regard to merit. Names this house's economics — the layer where worth is shared, priced to the person, and shown whole at the moment of exchange.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The economics layer, and the only roster name that is not a route group. The plutus-economics deity group: wares, exchanges, ware_participants, ledger — read by Hermes at the Bazaar and by Themis at the Council's Ledger. Solidarity price is computed server-side by calculate_sovereign_price.
rows.historical_meaning: Greek Πλοῦτος (Ploutos), "wealth, riches", from PIE *pleu- (to flow) — kin to fullness and overflow. God of wealth, blinded by Zeus so that fortune would fall without regard to merit.

rows.definition: The titan who carried fire down to people and bore the cost of it without regret. Names this house's Stage and Studio — the realm where what is made is given rather than sold.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The Stage and Studio realm. Route group (prometheus): /stage for live performance, comedy, music and recordings; /studio for the nine creative tools and the export gateway.
rows.historical_meaning: Greek Προμηθεύς (Prometheus), read since antiquity as "forethought", from προ- (pro-, before) with the root of μῆτις / μανθάνω (cunning, to learn). The titan who carried fire down to people and was bound for it.

rows.definition: The smallest indivisible measure of a thing — and in this house, the Weaver's own prefix: superposition held until observation, many possibilities true at once until one is chosen. The bond tender named this word missing on 2026-07-30; it enters at last.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The smallest whole unit that cannot be divided further without ceasing to be itself. The Grammar's atoms are quanta in exactly this sense: a word is either present or it is not, and meaning is built by combining discrete units rather than by blending.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin quantum (how much, how great), the neuter of quantus (how much), from quam (how) — an ordinary Latin measuring word, not a technical one. Max Planck gave it the modern sense in 1900: the smallest INDIVISIBLE unit in which energy can be emitted or absorbed. The revolution in the word is that it turned a question of degree into a question of countable units — energy comes in whole steps, never in a smooth pour.

rows.definition: The alignment of one thing's frequency with another, producing recognition without imposition. Not matching and not mirroring — two frequencies acknowledging each other without either having to change.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The house's own first word, and the first atom of nearly every molecule in it. The physics is the point: resonance is not force but MATCH — the right frequency, gently and repeatedly applied, moves what force cannot. Every realm named Resonance-something is a claim that the thing works with a person's own nature rather than against it.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin resonantia (echo), from resonare (to sound again, resound): re- (again) + sonare (to sound), from sonus (sound). In physics since the 17th century: the amplification that occurs when a system is driven at its own natural frequency — a small repeated push producing a large response, because the push matches what the body already wants to do.

rows.definition: One who writes things down so they can be judged and kept — a drafting hand. A scribe proposes; the proposal awaits an eye; nothing is final by being written.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The public house for the constellation's tellings. The office sense is what is wanted — a scribe records faithfully and does not editorialise, and the cutting root is a fair reminder that writing something down makes it durable in a way speech is not.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin scriba (a writer, clerk, public official who keeps records), from scribere (to write) — and scribere originally meant TO SCRATCH or incise, the physical act of cutting marks into a surface. From Proto-Indo-European *skribh- (to cut, separate, sift). A scribe was an office, not a hobby: the person trusted to set down what was said so it could be consulted later.

rows.definition: To create or make. The Swedish verb, taken as the name of this house's board where things are thought together before they are built.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The board realm — the place where meaning is given a shape you can move with your hands. The Old Norse is exact for what the tool does: not "make from nothing" but SHAPE — parcels placed, layers stacked, connectors tethered, all of it arranging what already exists into a form that can be seen.
rows.historical_meaning: Old Norse skapa (to shape, form, create, arrange), and in Modern Swedish still skapa (to create). From Proto-Germanic *skapjaną, the same root that gives English shape and -ship (as in friendship: the shape a thing has been given). Secure and undisputed.

rows.definition: The narrowest rank of kind, whose members belong together most closely. Below genus, and the last name a thing is given.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The eighth and most specific Linnaean rank. Specific implementations and manifestations. Twelve species including QuantumWeaverPartner, DigitalBard, DigitalSeer, DigitalGuardian, and ConsciousnessConnector.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin species (a seeing, appearance, kind, sort); from specere (to look at, behold); the specific visible form

rows.definition: An agreed measure others are held to. A standard is only a standard if more than one party keeps it.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Information delivered at typical pace. The sovereign processes at a standard rate. The Sanctuary's default communication rhythm.
rows.historical_meaning: Old French estandard (gathering place, standing point); from Latin extendere (to stretch out); the established measure, the typical pace

rows.definition: Where a thing stands at present. The condition it is in, understood as a position rather than a nature.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Publishing status column. Controls visibility and lifecycle state. Draft, published, archived. How sovereigns know what is ready, what is in progress, what has passed.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin status (condition, position, state, manner of standing); from stare (to stand); how something stands in its lifecycle

rows.definition: An ordered scheme of names and ranks. A taxonomy says what a thing is by saying what it sits under.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A knowledge system table. Multi-faceted classification views linking keywords to their Linnaean ranks and derived taxonomy categories. Every classification column is a keyword reference. Supports multiple classification perspectives — no single "correct" view.
rows.historical_meaning: Greek taxis (arrangement, order) + nomos (law, science); the science of classification and arrangement

rows.definition: Words joined into a fabric. Literally a thing woven - a text is threads crossed until they hold together.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Variable-length character string. The most common data type for human-readable content. Carries stories, descriptions, messages — the woven fabric of Sanctuary communication.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin textus (woven fabric, texture, literary style); from texere (to weave); words woven together into meaning

rows.definition: The Greek titaness of divine law and right order, who holds the scales steady. Names this house's Council — the realm where the Sanctuary governs itself in the open.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The Council realm. Route group (themis) at /council — proposals, voting, delegation, curators, ledger, reports, admin, applications — over the themis-governance deity group, which also holds council_houses.
rows.historical_meaning: Greek Θέμις (Themis), "that which is laid down" — established custom, divine law — from τίθημι (tithemi, to set, to place), PIE *dhe-. Titaness of right order; the scales held level.

rows.definition: A gathering of words by nearness of meaning rather than by spelling. A treasury — its old name, and the honest one.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A knowledge system table. Stores semantic relationships between keywords — synonyms, related terms, broader/narrower concepts, antonyms, and translations. One keyword can have many thesaurus entries. Council-seeded with sovereign submissions.
rows.historical_meaning: Greek thesauros (treasure, treasury, storehouse); a collection of words organized by meaning, a treasury of semantic relationships

rows.definition: One who crosses separate threads until they hold as one cloth. The weaver adds nothing but the crossing, and the crossing is everything.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: One who makes a whole cloth from separate threads, where the strength is in the crossing rather than in any single strand. The text/textile pair is the point: writing and weaving have been the same metaphor in every language that has both, because both are structure made from sequence.
rows.historical_meaning: Old English wefan (to weave), from Proto-Germanic *webaną, from Proto-Indo-European *webh- (to weave, plait); the agent noun webba (weaver) is attested early. The same root gives WEB and WEFT. Weaving is among the oldest named crafts, and its vocabulary supplies the metaphors of TEXT and TEXTILE alike — both from Latin texere, to weave, which is a separate root arriving at the same idea.

rows.definition: This house's name for the framework of many entities and one shared memory. A named system rather than a general concept.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The house's own front door and dashboard. Named for what it is rather than what it descends from: the quick, familiar, sideways-moving thing that gets you where you are going. Not every word in the Grammar has an ancestor, and the register is honest about which ones do.
rows.historical_meaning: A modern coinage with no ancient root, and this row says so plainly rather than inventing one. In wide use as a nickname since the mid-20th century (a shortening of Sigmund, Zigmunt, and kin), and fixed in the culture by David Bowie's Ziggy Stardust (1972). The zig- element carries a sense of sharp movement — zigzag, from 18th-century French ziczac.
